note:
The patient is a 72-year-old male seen in the psychiatry specialty clinic for follow-up of generalized anxiety disorder. He describes excessive worry about his finances and his health on most days for over a year, along with muscle tension and difficulty falling asleep. He feels restless in the evenings. He denies low mood, denies panic attacks, and denies any thoughts of harming himself. He does not drink alcohol. His only other medical problem is hypertension, which his primary care physician manages. He takes over-the-counter melatonin 3 mg at bedtime and several herbal products from a health food store, but he is unsure of their names and of what else is in them.

On examination today his blood pressure was 132/78 and his heart rate was 72. He was cooperative with a mildly anxious affect and a linear thought process, and there was no psychomotor agitation. His GAD-7 score was 14.

My impression is generalized anxiety disorder of moderate severity with associated sleep difficulty. After discussing the options, we agreed to start escitalopram 5 mg daily. I will order a basic metabolic panel in two weeks because older adults are at risk of low sodium on this type of medication. I asked him to bring all of his supplement bottles to the next visit and not to add any new supplements without checking with the clinic first. He will also be referred for cognitive behavioral therapy and will return in four weeks.
summary: A 72-year-old male with hypertension was seen in a psychiatry specialty clinic for follow-up of generalized anxiety disorder. He reported excessive worry on most days for over a year with muscle tension, restlessness and difficulty falling asleep, and he denied low mood, panic attacks and thoughts of harming himself. He takes over-the-counter melatonin and several unidentified herbal products. His GAD-7 score was 14 and the only notable finding was a mildly anxious affect. The impression was moderate generalized anxiety disorder with sleep difficulty, and escitalopram 5 mg daily was started with a basic metabolic panel in two weeks, a supplement review, a cognitive behavioral therapy referral and follow-up in four weeks.

note:
Cardiology clinic new patient visit, dictating. This is a 54-year-old male referred by his primary care physician for evaluation of palpitations. He reports about three months of episodes where his heart feels like it is racing and fluttering, occurring roughly twice a week, lasting five to ten minutes, correction, five to twenty minutes, and usually coming on in the evening when he is resting. He had mild lightheadedness with two of the episodes. He denies chest pain, denies syncope, denies shortness of breath, and denies leg swelling. He drinks about three cups of coffee a day and two beers on the weekend. There is no history of thyroid disease and no family history of sudden cardiac death. Past medical history includes HTN and hyperlipidemia. Current medications are amlodipine 5 mg once daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly.

Vitals today, blood pressure 142/88, heart rate 76, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, weight 92 kilograms. On exam he is well appearing. Regular rate and rhythm with occasional extra beats, normal S1 and S2, no murmurs, lungs clear, no peripheral edema, no jugular venous distension. ECG today shows normal sinus rhythm at 74 with occasional premature atrial contractions, normal intervals and no pre-excitation. Labs from his primary care visit last month show TSH 1.9, hemoglobin 14.8, potassium 4.2 and creatinine 0.9.

Impression number one, palpitations most likely due to premature atrial contractions, with caffeine and alcohol as likely triggers, and we need to rule out paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Number two, HTN, above goal today. Number three, hyperlipidemia, stable. Plan, a 14-day patch monitor, a transthoracic echocardiogram, and a magnesium level. I am starting metoprolol succinate 25 mg once daily for both the palpitations and the blood pressure, and he will continue amlodipine 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg. I advised cutting caffeine to one cup daily and limiting alcohol. He should call or go to the emergency department for fainting or chest pain. Return to clinic in four weeks to review the monitor and echo results.

He denied chest pain, syncope, shortness of breath and leg swelling, and drinks three cups of coffee a day. Blood pressure was 142/88, and the ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with occasional premature atrial contractions; TSH, hemoglobin, potassium and creatinine were normal. The impression was palpitations from premature atrial contractions, with HTN above goal. Metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily was started, a 14-day patch monitor, echocardiogram and magnesium level were ordered, and follow-up is in four weeks.

note:
The patient is an 84-year-old male on hospital day 4 after a fall from standing height at home that caused a left femoral neck fracture, which was repaired with a hemiarthroplasty on hospital day 1. Geriatrics was asked to see him for bone health and fracture prevention. His daughter, who is his main caregiver and lives with him, is at the bedside and provided much of the history because he is hard of hearing and sometimes forgets details. She reports that he has lost several centimeters of height over the past few years and that he fractured his right wrist two years ago after tripping on a rug. He has never had a bone density scan and has never been treated for osteoporosis. He has never smoked, drinks very little alcohol, and has had no long-term steroid use. His history includes benign prostatic hyperplasia, for which he takes tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly, and he also takes calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily on his own. He has no known drug allergies.

Today he denies chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, and fever. He has moderate pain at the left hip that is controlled with acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed. His daughter says his appetite has been fair, but he has eaten less than usual since the fall.

Vitals this morning were temperature 36.9 C, blood pressure 128/74, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He is alert and pleasant but hard of hearing. The surgical incision is clean, dry, and intact with no erythema, and there is no calf tenderness. Labs show calcium 9.0 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, 25-hydroxy vitamin D 14 ng/mL, TSH 2.1, and hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL.

My impression is osteoporosis with a hip fragility fracture and a prior wrist fragility fracture, along with vitamin D deficiency. He is receiving clot prophylaxis through orthopedics. I recommend starting vitamin D3 2000 units daily now and continuing calcium carbonate and acetaminophen. Once his vitamin D is replete, I plan to give zoledronic acid 5 mg IV at his first geriatrics follow-up visit, provided his kidney function remains normal. We will obtain a DXA scan as an outpatient for a baseline and arrange physical therapy and a home safety evaluation. I reviewed the plan with the patient and his daughter, and she verbalized understanding.

He had lost height, had a prior wrist fracture and had never been treated for osteoporosis, and he denied chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea and fever. Vitamin D was 14 ng/mL and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. The impression was osteoporosis with hip and wrist fragility fractures and vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D3 2000 units daily was started, zoledronic acid 5 mg IV is planned once vitamin D is replete, and an outpatient DXA scan and physical therapy were arranged.

note:
60-year-old female, new pt, pulm clinic. Referred by PCP for chronic cough x 4 mo.
Limited health literacy per pt (reads "a little", sister usually helps w/ forms). Used plain language + teach-back throughout. Pt brought all pill bottles in a grocery bag.

CC: cough "that won't go away" x ~4 mo
HPI:
- dry hacking cough daily, worse at night + when lying flat
- occasional clear phlegm in AM
- c/o tickle in throat, frequent throat clearing
- c/o heartburn + sour taste after dinner 3-4x/wk
- DOE x 1 flight of stairs, unchanged x 1 yr
- tried OTC cough syrup + honey, no help
- denies hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, wt loss
- denies wheeze, denies orthopnea, no leg swelling
- no sick contacts, no recent URI, no known TB exposure

PMH: HTN, T2DM, GERD
Social: current smoker, 1 ppd x 35 yr = 35 pk-yr. "Thinking about quitting maybe." No EtOH. Works as a cashier.
Allergies: NKDA

Meds - pt first states: lisinopril 10 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BID, omeprazole 20 mg daily, albuterol PRN.
Bottles reviewed: lisinopril bottle reads 20 mg daily (filled ~6 mo ago, cough started ~4 mo ago). CORRECTION: lisinopril is 20 mg daily, not 10 mg. Metformin 500 mg BID and omeprazole 20 mg daily confirmed on bottles. Albuterol HFA 2 puffs q4-6h PRN, uses ~1x/wk.

Vitals: BP 148/86, HR 82, RR 18, SpO2 96% RA, temp 98.4 F, wt 182 lb, BMI 31
Exam: NAD, speaks full sentences. Mild throat cobblestoning, no pharyngeal exudate. Lungs CTA b/l, no wheeze/crackles, no clubbing. Heart RRR. No LE edema.

Data:
- Spirometry today: FEV1 2.4 L (88% pred), FVC 3.0 L, FEV1/FVC 0.80, no obstruction
- CXR 2 views: lungs clear, no mass, no infiltrate
- Labs (PCP, last mo): A1c 7.4, Cr 0.9, K 4.3, eGFR 82, WBC 8.1

Imp:
1. Chronic cough x 4 mo, likely ACE inhibitor-induced cough from lisinopril +/- GERD; asthma and COPD less likely w/ nl spirometry
2. HTN, above goal today
3. GERD, sx not controlled
4. T2DM, A1c 7.4
5. Tobacco use disorder, 35 pk-yr, eligible for LDCT screening

Plan:
- STOP lisinopril 20 mg daily today
- START losartan 50 mg daily
- BMP in 1-2 wk after switch (K, Cr)
- INCREASE omeprazole 20 mg -> 40 mg daily, take 30 min before dinner; raise HOB, no food 3 hr before bed
- cont metformin 500 mg BID
- cont albuterol 2 puffs q4-6h PRN
- smoking cessation counseling ~5 min; START nicotine patch 21 mg/24 h daily; quitline referral given
- LDCT chest ordered for lung cancer screening
- teach-back done: pt named which pill to stop; gave large-print picture med list; sister to be called w/ plan
- expect cough to ease in 1-4 wk after stopping ACE inhibitor, may take up to 3 mo
- f/u 6 wk. RTC sooner or ED for hemoptysis, fever, or worsening SOB
- if cough persists at f/u: CT chest, further GERD workup
summary: A 60-year-old female with HTN, T2DM, GERD and current tobacco use was seen for chronic cough of four months, with limited health literacy addressed using plain language and teach-back. She had a dry hacking cough worse at night, throat clearing and heartburn, and denied hemoptysis, fever, night sweats and weight loss. Bottle review corrected her lisinopril dose to 20 mg daily; spirometry and chest X-ray were unremarkable. The impression was likely ACE inhibitor-induced cough with possible GERD. Lisinopril was stopped, losartan 50 mg daily and a nicotine patch were started, omeprazole was increased to 40 mg daily, and a BMP, low-dose chest CT and six-week follow-up were planned.

The patient is a 42-year-old female on postpartum day 2 after a repeat low transverse cesarean delivery at term. She delivered a healthy infant and is breastfeeding well. Overnight she slept in short stretches and reports incisional pain of 4 out of 10 that is controlled with her current regimen. She is ambulating in the hallway, voiding spontaneously, passing flatus, and tolerating a regular diet. She denies fever, denies heavy vaginal bleeding, denies calf pain, denies headache or visual changes, and denies chest pain or shortness of breath. She reports mild lightheadedness when she first stands up. She has no known drug allergies.

Vital signs this morning were temperature 37.1 C, blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 84, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On examination the fundus is firm at the umbilicus, lochia is moderate and rubra, and the incision is clean, dry, and intact with no erythema or drainage. Lungs are clear and there is no calf tenderness. Hemoglobin this morning was 8.9 g/dL compared with 11.6 g/dL before delivery, white count 11.4, and platelets 210. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score was 3.

Impression is postpartum day 2 after cesarean delivery with expected recovery, and postpartum anemia from blood loss. For pain control, oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed was stopped because she has needed none in 24 hours, and she will continue ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours and acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours. Ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily is started for the anemia. She is interested in a copper IUD and will return at six weeks postpartum for placement. Lactation support continues. If her hemoglobin is stable and she remains well, we anticipate discharge tomorrow with a blood pressure check and an incision check in one to two weeks.

note:
The patient is a 32-year-old female with ulcerative colitis on hospital day 3, admitted with a moderate flare after two weeks of worsening bloody diarrhea despite outpatient mesalamine. On admission she was having eight loose stools a day with visible blood and lower abdominal cramping. Since starting intravenous methylprednisolone 40 mg daily her stool frequency has fallen to three per day, and she saw blood only once yesterday. She denies fever, denies vomiting, and denies nocturnal stools for the past two nights. She has no abdominal pain at rest today. She reports mild fatigue. She has no known drug allergies and does not smoke.

Vital signs this morning were temperature 36.8 C, blood pressure 112/70, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 14, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The abdomen is soft and non-distended with mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant, no guarding, and normal bowel sounds. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile was negative on admission. C-reactive protein has fallen from 48 to 14 mg/L, hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL with a low ferritin, and albumin is 3.4 g/dL. Flexible sigmoidoscopy on admission showed continuous friable, erythematous mucosa with erosions from the rectum to 30 cm, consistent with a Mayo endoscopic score of 2.

Impression is a moderate ulcerative colitis flare that is responding to steroids, with iron deficiency anemia. Because she flared on mesalamine alone, she needs step-up maintenance therapy. We will stop intravenous methylprednisolone today and start prednisone 40 mg daily by mouth with a planned taper over eight weeks. She will continue mesalamine 2.4 g daily. I recommend starting vedolizumab 300 mg IV as maintenance therapy before discharge, and I have sent QuantiFERON and hepatitis B surface antigen testing, which must be reviewed before the first infusion. Ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily is started for the iron deficiency. If she continues to improve, she can go home tomorrow with outpatient gastroenterology follow-up in two weeks.

She denies fever, vomiting and nocturnal stools. C. difficile testing was negative, C-reactive protein fell from 48 to 14 mg/L, hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL, and sigmoidoscopy showed a Mayo score of 2. The impression is a steroid-responsive moderate ulcerative colitis flare with iron deficiency anemia. Methylprednisolone is changed to prednisone 40 mg daily with a taper, mesalamine continues, ferrous sulfate is started, and vedolizumab is planned once QuantiFERON and hepatitis B testing are reviewed.

note:
The patient is a 73-year-old male on hospital day 2 for acute urinary retention due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. A professional medical interpreter was used for the entire visit. He reports several years of a weak stream, hesitancy, a sense of incomplete emptying, and getting up four times each night to urinate. Three weeks ago his primary care physician started oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for urgency, and over the past week he passed progressively less urine until he could not void at all on the day of admission. He denies fever, denies dysuria, denies visible blood in the urine, and denies flank pain. He has hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

On arrival a bladder scan showed 780 mL, and a Foley catheter returned 800 mL of clear yellow urine. Urine output since then has been good, about 1.8 liters over the past 24 hours, without hematuria. Vital signs this morning were temperature 36.7 C, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 74, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The suprapubic area is non-tender and no longer distended. A digital rectal exam shows a smooth, symmetric, enlarged prostate without nodules. Creatinine was 1.4 mg/dL on admission and 1.0 mg/dL today. Urinalysis showed trace leukocyte esterase with no nitrites, and the culture is negative so far. PSA was 3.8 ng/mL. Renal and bladder ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis and an estimated prostate volume of 62 mL.

Impression is acute urinary retention caused by benign prostatic hyperplasia and likely precipitated by the anticholinergic oxybutynin, with a mild acute kidney injury that has resolved. I stopped the oxybutynin and started tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily after dinner. We will add finasteride 5 mg daily given the large prostate. Amlodipine continues. A trial without catheter is planned for tomorrow morning after three doses of tamsulosin, with a bladder scan afterward. I reviewed all of this with the patient through the interpreter, and he confirmed his understanding by teach-back. He will see the urology clinic in four weeks.
summary: A 73-year-old male with hypertension was admitted on hospital day 2 with acute urinary retention due to benign prostatic hyperplasia, with a professional interpreter used for the visit. He had a weak stream, hesitancy, nocturia four times nightly and recent oxybutynin use, and he denied fever, dysuria, visible hematuria and flank pain. A Foley catheter drained 800 mL, creatinine improved from 1.4 to 1.0 mg/dL, PSA was 3.8 ng/mL, and ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis and a 62 mL prostate. Oxybutynin was stopped, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily and finasteride 5 mg daily were started, a trial without catheter is planned tomorrow, and urology follow-up is in four weeks.

note:
The patient is a 36-year-old female on hospital day 2 for an upper gastrointestinal bleed from a duodenal ulcer. She presented with two days of black, tarry stools and lightheadedness after several weeks of taking ibuprofen 600 mg two to three times a day for tension headaches. She works rotating night and day shifts at a distribution center, sleeps at irregular times, and often skips meals, which she believes made her headaches worse. She denies vomiting blood, denies chest pain, denies abdominal pain at the moment, and denies alcohol use. She has no known drug allergies.

Overnight she had no further black stools and no change in her condition. Her admission hemoglobin was 7.2 g/dL and she received one unit of packed red blood cells, after which it rose to 8.4 g/dL this morning. Vital signs today were blood pressure 112/68, heart rate 86, respiratory rate 16, temperature 36.9 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. BUN was 28, creatinine 0.7, platelets 280, and INR 1.0. On exam she is pale but comfortable, the abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no rebound, and there is no active bleeding. EGD on the day of admission found an 8 mm duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel that was treated with epinephrine injection and two hemoclips, and gastric biopsies were sent for Helicobacter pylori.

Impression is an upper gastrointestinal bleed from an NSAID-associated duodenal ulcer, status post endoscopic hemostasis, with acute blood loss anemia that is stable. Pantoprazole 40 mg IV twice daily will continue for 72 hours and then be changed to 40 mg orally twice daily. Nurse: Okay, you're in room three. Your blood pressure is 118 over 76, pulse 82, temperature 98.2.
Doctor: Thank you, and welcome to urgent care. So I have you down as a 36-year-old female with pelvic pain that keeps coming back. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: It's been about two years now. It's low in my belly, kind of on both sides, and it gets really bad right before and during my period. Today it's worse than usual, like a seven out of ten.
Doctor: Does it happen at other times of the month?
Patient: More and more, yeah. Some days it just aches all the time. And it hurts when I have sex, deep inside. It also hurts when I go to the bathroom during my period.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No, none.
Doctor: Any unusual discharge, burning when you urinate, or bleeding between periods?
Patient: No discharge, no burning, and no bleeding in between. My periods are heavy, but they come on time.
Doctor: Any nausea or vomiting?
Patient: No.
Doctor: What have you been taking for the pain?
Patient: Ibuprofen, 400 milligrams, maybe twice a day when it's bad. It only helps a little. I've been to the ER and to urgent care a few times, and they told me my tests were fine.
Doctor: Any surgeries, other health problems, or allergies to medicines?
Patient: No surgeries, nothing else, and no allergies.
Doctor: Have you seen a gynecologist?
Patient: I made an appointment once, but I don't have a car, and the bus takes almost two hours each way, so I missed it. I've missed two others for the same reason.
Doctor: That's a real barrier, and I want to build the plan around it. Your urine pregnancy test is negative and your urinalysis shows no infection. On exam your lower belly is tender on both sides, but there is no rebound and no guarding. On the pelvic exam you have tenderness behind the uterus and some firmness along the ligaments, there is no cervical motion tenderness, and no discharge. Altogether, my working diagnosis is chronic pelvic pain, and I suspect endometriosis.
Patient: Is that serious?
Doctor: It's common and treatable, but we should confirm it. First, increase your ibuprofen to 600 milligrams every six hours with food for the next week. Second, I'm starting norethindrone acetate 5 milligrams once a day, taken continuously, and I'll write for a 90-day supply so you don't need a ride for refills. Third, I'm ordering a transvaginal ultrasound, and our social worker will give you a ride voucher for it. Your gynecology follow-up will be a video visit so you don't have to travel. Go to the emergency room for a fever, heavy bleeding, or severe pain that doesn't ease.
Patient: Okay, that works for me. Thank you.

The urine pregnancy test and urinalysis were negative, and she had bilateral lower abdominal tenderness and tenderness behind the uterus without rebound or guarding. The working diagnosis is chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis. Ibuprofen was increased, norethindrone acetate was started, a transvaginal ultrasound was ordered, and follow-up will be by video because of transportation barriers.

Doctor: Come on in and have a seat. Thanks for coming. So you're a 31-year-old female, and you're here because you think you might have ADHD. Is that right?
Patient: Yeah. I keep forgetting stuff and I can't finish things. My sister said I should get checked.
Doctor: Tell me what that looks like day to day.
Patient: Like, I start a bunch of things and don't finish. I lose my keys and my phone every day. At work I zone out in meetings and I miss deadlines. I'm always late. It was the same in school, the teachers said I daydreamed all the time.
Doctor: Did this start when you were a kid?
Patient: Yeah, since I was little. My mom said I was always in my own world.
Doctor: Do you feel restless, like you can't sit still?
Patient: A little inside, like my mind is going. But I can sit.
Doctor: Any times when you had super high energy and barely slept for days?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Any thoughts of hurting yourself?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Any chest pain, racing heart, or fainting?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Any seizures?
Patient: No. And no drugs. Maybe a glass of wine on weekends.
Doctor: Okay. Now let's go over your medicines. I know reading is hard for you, so show me what you have on your phone.
Patient: Okay. I take the sertraline, 50 milligrams, one in the morning. It's for my anxiety.
Doctor: Can you look at the photo of the bottle and read me the number?
Patient: Oh. It says 100 milligrams, one tablet each morning. I was thinking of the old dose. My doctor raised it last year.
Doctor: Good catch. So sertraline 100 milligrams every morning. What else?
Patient: The inhaler, albuterol, two puffs when I wheeze. The montelukast, 10 milligrams at night, for my asthma. The iron pills, ferrous sulfate, 325 milligrams, twice a day, and they upset my stomach. And at night I take Benadryl, 25 milligrams, to sleep.
Nurse: Vitals today are blood pressure 130 over 84, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Doctor: Thank you. Your labs from last week show a ferritin of 12, which is low, hemoglobin 11.2, and a normal TSH of 2.4. Your ECG today is normal, sinus rhythm at 78, and your urine drug screen was negative. The ASRS questions we read together were positive.
Doctor: So here's what I think. You have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, mostly the inattentive type. You also have asthma, anxiety, and iron deficiency. Here is the plan. First, I'm starting atomoxetine, 40 milligrams every morning. It's not a stimulant, which is safer with your blood pressure and anxiety, and we can raise it in two weeks. Second, stop the Benadryl. It can make attention worse, so keep the same bedtime and a dark room instead. Third, stop the montelukast. It can affect mood and sleep, and I'll message your primary doctor about another way to control your asthma. Fourth, drop the iron to 325 milligrams once a day so it bothers your stomach less, and we'll recheck the ferritin in three months. Keep taking the sertraline, 100 milligrams every morning, and the albuterol when you wheeze.
Patient: That's a lot.
Doctor: It is, so tell me back in your own words what's changing.
Patient: Stop the Benadryl and the montelukast. Start the new one in the morning. Iron one time, not two. Sertraline stays the same.
Doctor: Perfect. I'll give you a picture pill card and call your sister with your permission. Come back in two weeks and we'll check your blood pressure and heart rate.
summary: A 31-year-old female with limited reading ability was evaluated for adult ADHD after a lifelong pattern of forgetfulness, lost items, zoning out and missed deadlines. Ferritin was 12, hemoglobin 11.2, TSH 2.4, and the ECG and urine drug screen were normal. The impression was attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with asthma, anxiety and iron deficiency. Atomoxetine 40 milligrams every morning was started, Benadryl and montelukast were stopped, iron was reduced to once a day, and follow-up is in two weeks.

note:
Nurse: Vitals are in. Temperature 99.1, pulse 108, blood pressure 124 over 76, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She rates her pain a nine out of ten.
Doctor: Thanks. I'm the doctor here at urgent care today. I understand you're a 34-year-old female with sickle cell disease and you're having one of your pain crises. Tell me what's happening.
Patient: It started yesterday after my shift. It's in my low back and both legs, that deep, gnawing pain, same as my other crises. I couldn't sleep at all.
Doctor: How does it compare with your usual crises?
Patient: About the same, maybe a little worse. I work nights in a hotel kitchen and some weeks they switch me to days, so I've barely slept and I haven't been drinking much water. I felt warm last night.
Doctor: Any chest pain or trouble breathing?
Patient: No, no chest pain. My breathing's okay.
Doctor: Any cough?
Patient: No cough.
Doctor: Any weakness, numbness, vision changes, or trouble speaking?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Any vomiting or belly pain?
Patient: No vomiting, no belly pain.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking?
Patient: Hydroxyurea, 500 milligrams, twice a day. Folic acid, one milligram every day. Oxycodone, 10 milligrams every four hours when the pain is bad. And ibuprofen, 600 milligrams, when it's really bad.
Doctor: Is that right? That sounds like a lot of oxycodone.
Patient: Oh, wait, I got that wrong. The hydroxyurea is two 500 capsules once a day, so 1000 total. And the oxycodone is the 5 milligram, one tablet every six hours when needed. I keep mixing them up.
Doctor: Okay, so hydroxyurea 1000 milligrams once a day and oxycodone 5 milligrams every six hours as needed. Thank you. How often do you take the ibuprofen?
Patient: Maybe three or four days a week.
Doctor: And how much alcohol do you drink?
Patient: After shifts, honestly, about six drinks most nights, to relax. I know it's a lot.
Doctor: I appreciate you being honest. Let me examine you. You look uncomfortable but you're alert. You have mild scleral icterus, which is usual for you. Your lungs are clear. Your heart is fast but regular. You're tender over the low back and both thighs, with no joint swelling or redness. Your belly is soft and not tender, and there is no weakness on exam.
Doctor: While you were resting, I gave you hydromorphone 2 milligrams IV, twice, thirty minutes apart, and a liter of IV fluids.
Patient: The pain is down to a three now.
Doctor: Good. We checked a blood count, reticulocytes, and a metabolic panel. Your hemoglobin is 7.6, close to your baseline of about 8. Your white count is 14.2, platelets 410. Your creatinine is 1.3, and your usual is 0.9. The liver tests are mildly up, ALT 62 and AST 88. Your chest X-ray is clear, so no sign of acute chest syndrome.
Doctor: Here's my impression. This is a sickle cell pain crisis, probably set off by lack of sleep and dehydration. You also have a mild acute kidney injury, which the ibuprofen and dehydration likely made worse, and heavy alcohol use that is affecting your liver tests. You're safe to go home. First, stop the ibuprofen completely. Second, keep the oxycodone 5 milligrams every six hours as needed. Third, you can add acetaminophen, 500 milligrams every six hours as needed, but no more than 2 grams a day because of the alcohol. Fourth, because you're having frequent crises, I want to raise the hydroxyurea from 1000 to 1500 milligrams once a day, and continue the folic acid. Fifth, start thiamine, 100 milligrams once a day. Sixth, drink at least three liters of water a day, and I'm referring you for alcohol treatment support.
Patient: My schedule changes every week, so I never know when I can come in.
Doctor: Then call the hematology clinic today with this week's shifts and they'll book a late-day visit with a repeat metabolic panel in three days. Come back right away for chest pain, trouble breathing, fever over 101, weakness, or vision changes.
Patient: Okay, I understand. Thank you.
summary: A 34-year-old female shift worker with sickle cell disease and heavy alcohol use presented with a pain crisis in the low back and both legs, 9 out of 10, after poor sleep and dehydration. She denied chest pain, trouble breathing, cough, weakness, numbness, vision changes, vomiting and belly pain, and corrected her hydroxyurea and oxycodone doses. Hemoglobin was 7.6, creatinine 1.3, the chest X-ray was clear, and pain fell to 3 out of 10 after two doses of IV hydromorphone and fluids. The impression was a sickle cell pain crisis with mild acute kidney injury. Ibuprofen was stopped, hydroxyurea was raised to 1500 milligrams daily, acetaminophen and thiamine were added, and hematology follow-up was arranged around her shifts.
